children: Bokaro sits about 300 km from the Haldia and Kolkata ports, but Harsh Bansal says export success in coated steel will depend on consistent quality, international certifications, traceability and dependable delivery

India’s primary steel producers are racing towards 300 million tonnes of capacity by 2030-31, and the question for the industry is who turns that steel into products customers can actually use. For Harsh Bansal, managing director (MD) of BMW Industries, that conversion layer is where the next phase of value will be created, through application-specific products, just-in-time delivery, quality assurance and technical support.

In this interview, Bansal explains how that expansion changes the company’s product mix and customer base, and which emerging sectors, from data centres and shipbuilding to defence and EV manufacturing, will drive demand for value-added steel. He also sets out the policy measures that would strengthen downstream manufacturing beyond trade protection, from SME credit to PLI-type support, what it will take for Indian coated steel to compete in export markets, and why skilling and lower-carbon processing must grow alongside physical capacity.

As primary producers expand towards 300 million tonnes of capacity by 2030-31, how does the role of an independent processing partner evolve? Where does the next layer of value in that partnership sit?

As primary steel producers scale up, the role of independent processors becomes increasingly important as the conversion layer between steel production and the specific requirements of end customers. The opportunity is no longer only about processing volumes, but about delivering the right specification, quality, consistency and turnaround for different applications.

We see the next layer of value coming from customised, application-specific products, just-in-time delivery, quality assurance and technical support, along with flexibility. This also changes the workforce requirement. Downstream processing needs process engineers, metallurgists, quality specialists and skilled operators who can manage increasingly sophisticated processes. Our association with TSL & SAIL is an example of how primary producers and downstream processors can complement each other, combining scale with specialised processing capabilities and customer proximity.
Your Bokaro complex adds cold rolled, galvanised and colour-coated capacity alongside your SAIL joint venture. How does that change your product mix and the customers you can serve as it ramps up?

The Bokaro complex will allow us to move further towards value-added and application-driven steel products. With cold rolled, Galvalume, Galvanised and colour-coated capabilities, our product mix can address customers who require greater consistency, surface quality and specific performance characteristics rather than only basic steel processing. This opens up opportunities across sectors such as appliances, automotive, construction, pre-engineered buildings, roofing and cladding, as well as organised OEMs that require reliable coated steel quality. As the facility ramps up, the focus will be on capacity utilisation and increasing the contribution of value-added products.

There is also an important workforce dimension. Coating and finishing operations require specialised skills in process control, quality inspection and surface treatment. Building these capabilities locally through hiring and training will be an important part of developing the Bokaro ecosystem.

Finished steel consumption grew 8.3 per cent in the first quarter of FY27. Beyond infrastructure and housing, which emerging sectors, such as data centres, shipbuilding and defence, will drive the next leg of demand for value-added steel?

The next phase of steel demand is likely to be increasingly driven by sectors where specifications, quality and traceability matter as much as volumes. Data centres, for instance, require steel across structural applications, cladding, cabinets and racking. Shipbuilding and defence can create demand for specialised grades and materials that meet stringent quality and compliance requirements.

Solar structures, automotive and EV-related manufacturing, and white goods are other areas where demand for consistent, application-specific steel can grow. These markets favour organised processors that can provide reliable quality, testing and traceability.

India has put a three-year safeguard duty on flat steel imports, including galvanised and colour-coated products. Beyond trade protection, which policy measures would do the most to strengthen downstream steel and domestic manufacturing over the next decade?

Trade measures can provide the industry with some stability, but long-term competitiveness will require a broader ecosystem approach. For downstream processors, predictable access to raw materials at competitive prices is important because the economics of value-added processing are closely linked to input costs. Additionally, access to capital, i.e. sustainable debt funding costs, is increasingly critical to create capacities. With banks and institutions, flush with funds, they need to get aggressive with funding the SME sectors at competitive pricing, which thus is reserved for high rated clients, kind of creates a vicious cycle the small players face difficulty in getting out if.

There is also an opportunity to extend PLI-type support to more value-added downstream steel products, particularly where domestic manufacturing can replace imports and create export opportunities. Reducing logistics and power costs would further improve competitiveness, while faster certification and BIS processes can help manufacturers bring products to market more efficiently.

Skilling should be another important pillar. Industry-linked programmes with ITIs, polytechnics and technical institutions can help create a workforce trained specifically in steel processing, coating, quality control and automation. Over the next decade, building these capabilities alongside physical capacity will be critical. National Skill Development Mission is a great step in the right direction.
Bokaro sits about 300 kilometres from the Haldia and Kolkata ports. How big can exports become for Indian downstream steel, and what will it take to compete globally in coated products?

India has a significant opportunity to build a stronger export position in downstream and coated steel, particularly as global customers increasingly look for competitive, reliable and diversified supply chains. For facilities in the Bokaro region, proximity to the Kolkata and Haldia port ecosystem can support more efficient movement of products and improve the competitiveness of exports.

However, competing globally will require more than a freight advantage. Customers will expect consistent coating quality, international certifications, traceability and dependable delivery schedules. Building long-term relationships with overseas customers and developing strong product and brand positioning will also be important. Our focus is therefore on building the base for export competitiveness rather than looking at exports purely as a volume opportunity. As the infrastructure across the country improves, there will be greater opportunities in the future.
As customers and export markets look more closely at the carbon footprint of steel, how should processors approach the shift to higher-value, lower-carbon manufacturing?

For downstream processors, the transition to lower-carbon manufacturing is primarily about improving the efficiency of operations and making better choices across the value chain. This includes improving energy efficiency across processing lines, increasing the use of renewable power & other resources (water, etc.), where feasible, reducing scrap and material losses, improving yield and evaluating lower-impact coating processes. There is also an important upstream consideration. Processors can increasingly work with suppliers that are able to provide lower-carbon steel, particularly as customers and export markets seek greater visibility into the carbon footprint of their supply chains.
